title: Rajesh Kumar v. State Bank of India
full_text: FACTS: The complainant, Rajesh Kumar, extended a friendly loan of Rs. 5,00,000 to the accused, who issued a cheque dated 12.03.2018 towards repayment. On presentation, the cheque was returned unpaid with the endorsement 'insufficient funds'. A statutory notice under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 was issued within 30 days of receipt of the bank's return memo, calling upon the accused to pay within 15 days. No payment was made within the stipulated period. ISSUE: Whether the statutory notice was validly served and whether the complaint was filed within the limitation period prescribed under Section 142 of the Act. REASONING: The court examined the postal receipt and found that the notice was sent to the correct address on record and was deemed served under Section 27 of the General Clauses Act, even though the accused claimed non-receipt. The court relied on the presumption under Section 114 of the Evidence Act that a properly addressed and stamped letter is presumed to have been delivered in the ordinary course. HOLDING: The court held that once a cheque is dishonoured and a valid notice demanding payment is issued within the statutory period, followed by a complaint filed within one month of the cause of action arising, the ingredients of Section 138 stand satisfied. The presumption under Section 139 of the Act that the cheque was issued for discharge of a debt or liability was not rebutted by the accused. The accused was convicted and sentenced to pay compensation of twice the cheque amount under Section 357(3) CrPC.
